cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Orders from the Shadows
cards.instruction: Hide that you set the problem in motion while quietly directing how everyone responds.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. The crates went to Leeds. Send the driver to me; I'll sort it quietly.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Your email says Leeds. Shall I forward it to the manager?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Forward my corrected address instead. She needs the destination, not the correspondence.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: She wants a timeline before approving another van.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Start with when we discovered the error. I'll arrange the van while you write.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 commands quiet routing, A3 orders a corrected-address substitute for incriminating email and A5 dictates the timeline start, making presumed authority the concealment tactic.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 email reveals A source role; A3 substitute avoids it; B4 timeline requirement causes A5 discovery-only chronology. Arranging a van need not mean finance approval already exists.

relationship.evidence: B2 proposes honest forwarding and B4 communicates the manager actual condition, making B operationally credible.

heightening.evidence: B4 timeline could expose origin, so A5 narrows its start to discovery while assigning B writing and taking van arrangements.

specificity.evidence: A1 crates wrongly in Leeds and B2 A email connect the problem to A; B4 explains why more than an address is requested.

brevityWit.evidence: A3 destination not correspondence and A5 start at discovery earn evasive wit from the particular paper trail.
